dimensions.assessment: Affects domestic timber producers, sawmills, pulp and paper mills, homebuilders, federal agencies, and international trading partners.
dimensions.evidence: To strengthen American wood, and for other purposes.

dimensions.assessment: Substantially alters economic conditions through tax credits up to 5 times the base amount, multimillion-dollar state grants, and elimination of mill machinery tariffs.
dimensions.evidence: the amount of the credit determined under subsection (a) shall be equal to such amount (determined without regard to this sentence) multiplied by 5.

dimensions.assessment: Involves massive federal financial commitments including 95 percent of softwood lumber duties transferred to a new Build America Fund, multi-hundred-million-dollar state grants, and tax credit expansions.
dimensions.evidence: grant shall be not less than $100,000,000 and not greater than $200,000,000.

dimensions.assessment: Spans twelve federal departments and committees, enacting sweeping changes across tax policy, international trade, environmental standards, and federal procurement rules.
dimensions.evidence: The head of a Federal agency may not procure any hardwood, softwood, pulp, or a paper product... unless... derived solely from timber harvested and processed in the United States

dimensions.assessment: Permanent statutory updates to tax codes, permanent funds, and long-term regulatory changes, alongside provisions with 7-year sunset clauses for specific demonstration projects.
dimensions.evidence: The authority to carry out this section shall terminate on the date that is 7 years after the date of enactment of this section.

importance_detail.rationale: The Strong American Wood Act is a comprehensive, multi-title legislative package that introduces broad tax incentives, grants, trade investigations, retaliatory tariffs, and federal procurement mandates specifically aimed at strengthening the domestic wood, timber, and paper industries.

selection.reason: Impact scored and summarised by Gemini. (rated before the current eligibility rules; kept)

summary: H.R. 10906, titled the Strong American Wood Act, aims to support and strengthen the American timber, wood products, pulp, and paper industries through various tax incentives, research programs, trade restrictions, and regulatory updates. The bill establishes new tax credits for mass timber buildings and solid carbon capture, expands renewable biomass definitions, creates the Build America Fund funded by softwood lumber duties to provide grants for domestic single-family housing construction using local timber, updates definitions for plant biostimulants, directs demonstration and research projects for biochar and woody biomass, changes reforestation tax deduction rules, mandates federal procurement preferences for domestic forest products, requires trade investigations and potential retaliatory tariffs, eliminates mill machinery tariffs, revises the PM2.5 air quality standard, orders several supply chain assessments across federal agencies, and mandates secondary customs inspections for imported wood products.

affected_groups.effect: Receive expanded tax deductions for reforestation expenditures, increased disaster-related reforestation deductions, and increased market demand driven by domestic procurement mandates and housing grants.
affected_groups.group: Timber growers, loggers, and forestry businesses

affected_groups.effect: Benefit from the elimination of import tariffs on specific mill machinery, potential trade protections, and specific research and grant opportunities.
affected_groups.group: Sawmills, pulp mills, and paper mills

affected_groups.effect: Homebuilders and eligible homebuyers whose household income does not exceed 250 percent of the area median income can access repayable loans, down payment assistance, and credit enhancements through state revolving funds when constructing or purchasing single-family homes built with domestic timber.

Subject to stricter customs secondary inspections, potential trade investigations, retaliatory tariffs, and mandated domestic sourcing rules that restrict federal procurement of foreign-derived wood and paper.
affected_groups.group: Importers and foreign wood product producers

key_provisions: Establishes a mass timber buildings tax credit equal to $85 per metric ton of carbon dioxide stored in structural mass timber components, with increased amounts for projects meeting prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements.

Creates the Build America Fund, transferring past and future softwood lumber antidumping and countervailing duties to finance competitive grants for State housing finance agencies to operate revolving loan funds for single-family homes built with domestic timber.
Expands the Clean Air Act renewable biomass definition to include various manufacturing residuals and vegetation from non-federal, public, and tribal lands, as well as the wildland-urban interface.

Mandates that federal agencies procure hardwood, softwood, pulp, and paper products derived solely from timber harvested and processed in the United States, and updates the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act construction materials definition to include lumber, pulp, paper, and engineered wood.

Requires the Secretary of Commerce to conduct national security investigations under section 232 regarding imports of paper and wood, and instructs the U.S. Trade Representative to impose retaliatory tariffs against European Union member countries if they enforce certain deforestation or fumigant rules against U.S. products.
Directs the EPA Administrator to revise the national primary ambient air quality standard for PM2.5 from 9 micrograms per cubic meter to 12 micrograms per cubic meter within 90 days of enactment.

Eliminates all tariffs on specific machinery imported for use by sawmills, pulp mills, and paper mills, and requires U.S. Customs and Border Protection to conduct secondary inspections and documentation reviews for all imported wood products at ports of entry.
